title: Data poisoning
summary: An attacker writes a few documents so that retrieval returns them for chosen questions and the model repeats their false content. No hidden instruction is needed.
useIf: Anyone outside your editorial control can add or change content that gets indexed.
avoidIf: You need injection defences for hidden commands. Poisoning corrupts facts, so the controls differ.

explain.md: Poisoning attacks the **knowledge**, not the instructions. PoisonedRAG injected five malicious texts per target question into a knowledge base of millions of texts and reported a 90% attack success rate, and the defences the authors tested were insufficient [[r7]]. Scale does not dilute the attack: the planted text only has to outrank honest text for the targeted query.

OWASP LLM04 classes poisoning as an integrity attack and notes that embedding data can be manipulated, that external sources carry the highest risk and that a backdoor can stay dormant until a trigger appears [[tr3]]. MITRE ATLAS names the RAG cases: AML.T0070 RAG Poisoning and AML.T0071 False RAG Entry Injection [[r4]].

explain.title: A provenance gate before the index
explain.alt: Sources pass through authentication, a quarantine and review step, then are indexed with provenance fields and a trust tier that retrieval can filter on.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  S[Source] --> A[Authenticate writer]
  A --> Q[Quarantine and review]
  Q --> X[(Index with provenance and tier)]
  X --> R[Retrieval filters by tier]
  R --> C[Answer with citations]

explain.md: The controls follow the OWASP LLM08 list: validate data and authenticate sources, tag and classify combined data, and keep immutable retrieval logs [[r2]]. In practice that means recording who wrote each chunk, when and from which system, giving each source a **trust tier**, and letting high-stakes questions retrieve only from the curated tier. Showing citations lets a reader spot a strange source.

explain.title: Design reasoning, not a vendor feature
explain.md: Trust tiers, canary queries and corpus anomaly checks are patterns that follow from the sources above. No cited document prescribes these exact controls, so test them against your own corpus.

whereToUse: Corpora fed by forums, tickets, customer uploads or web crawls
Shared drives where many accounts can edit and a compromise would go unnoticed
Pipelines that re-ingest nightly from sources with weak change control
High-stakes answers such as policy, pricing, safety or legal guidance

use: Writers are many, mixed or external
A wrong answer has financial or safety impact
You can attach provenance at ingest
avoid: Relying on corpus size as protection
Treating a content-safety filter as a poisoning control: it looks for harm, not for false facts
Trusting a reranker to prefer honest text over text written to be relevant
flips: A single vetted team writes everything: focus on account compromise and review
Answers are low stakes and always cited: lighter tiering may be enough

pitfalls.symptom: An answer about one product changes with no deploy
pitfalls.cause: A new or edited chunk outranks the honest one for that query
pitfalls.fix: Compare retrieval logs with ingest provenance, and run golden questions after every ingest

pitfalls.cause: Copies live in caches, replicas or an old index version
pitfalls.fix: Delete by source id across index, caches and the previous blue-green index

pitfalls.symptom: No way to tell who wrote a chunk
pitfalls.cause: Provenance was not stored at ingest
pitfalls.fix: Store source, author, hash and ingest time as fields on every chunk

scenarios.title: Community forum as a source
scenarios.situation: A support assistant indexes an open customer community forum next to official documentation. Posts arrive all day. The assistant answers billing and safety questions.
unknowns: Can the forum be moderated before indexing?
scenarios.question: How do you design the index?

options.name: Moderate every post before it is indexed
options.tradeoff: Slow, costly, and plausible false content passes a quick review.

options.name: Separate trust tiers: official docs for high-stakes queries, forum content only for general help with citations
options.why: Poisoned posts cannot reach billing or safety answers, and the forum still adds recall elsewhere.
options.tradeoff: Some good forum answers are never used for strict questions.

options.name: One index and rely on the reranker to prefer good content
options.why: A reranker measures relevance, and planted text is written to be relevant.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only when every source is equally trusted and stakes are low.

flips.if: The forum is closed to verified staff
flips.then: Treat it as one tier with change logging.

flips.if: Answers are consumed by automation without a reader
flips.then: Make tiering strict and add golden-question checks.

scenarios.takeaway: Keep untrusted text away from decisions that cannot tolerate it.

scenarios.title: Small curated policy set
scenarios.situation: Two thousand policy documents are edited by around thirty vetted authors. Wrong answers carry legal risk. A compromised author account is the main worry.
unknowns: Is there change review in the source?
How fast must a poisoned change be reversible?
scenarios.question: What do you add?

options.name: Content safety filtering on every chunk
options.why: A false but polite policy statement is not harmful content, so it passes.
options.tradeoff: Useful for toxic content in open corpora, not for integrity.

options.name: Large embedding model upgrade
options.why: Better embeddings do not tell trusted text from planted text.
options.tradeoff: Right when recall is the problem, not integrity.

options.name: Reviewed, versioned changes, immutable ingest logs and a golden-question check after each ingest
options.why: A compromised account still needs a second reviewer, and any shifted answer is caught before users see it.
options.tradeoff: Slower publishing and a question set to maintain.

flips.if: Authors are numerous and change daily
flips.then: Add automated anomaly checks on newly retrieved chunks.

flips.if: Review is already enforced in the source system
flips.then: Mirror that review as an ingest condition and skip duplicate approval.

scenarios.takeaway: For a vetted corpus the threat is account compromise, so add review and regression checks.

scenarios.title: Web crawl at scale
scenarios.situation: A research assistant ingests millions of crawled pages across the open web. Reviewing each page is impossible. Answers cite sources.
unknowns: Are there domains you can trust more than others?
How costly is a wrong answer?
scenarios.question: What reduces risk most?

options.name: Domain trust scores with allowlisted tiers for sensitive topics, plus visible citations
options.why: It scales without per-page review and keeps readers in a position to judge.
options.tradeoff: Newer or niche sites lose recall in strict mode.

options.name: Add more documents so poison is diluted
options.why: PoisonedRAG reported 90% success with five texts among millions, so dilution does not work.
options.tradeoff: More data helps coverage, not integrity.

options.name: Manual spot checks of random pages
options.tradeoff: Random samples rarely hit the five texts aimed at one query.

flips.if: The assistant is used only for brainstorming
Targeted queries are known (brand or product names)
flips.then: Monitor those queries with golden answers.

scenarios.takeaway: Scale gives no protection against targeted poisoning.

quiz.q: Answers to refund questions changed on Tuesday. No deploy or model change happened. What do you check first?
options: Retrieval logs for the top chunks, joined to ingest provenance for anything new on that day
quiz.explain: A new or edited chunk that outranks the old one explains a change with no deploy. Temperature, prompt wording and latency do not explain a content shift that appeared on one day.

options: A few crafted texts among millions can steer answers for targeted questions
Poison only works on small corpora
Content safety filters block it reliably
It needs access to the model weights
quiz.explain: The paper reported 90% success with five malicious texts per target question in a knowledge base of millions, and the defences tested were insufficient. It does not need model access.

flashcards.front: How is data poisoning different from indirect injection?
flashcards.back: Poisoning plants false content that retrieval serves as fact. Injection plants instructions that the model may obey. Controls differ: provenance and review versus capability limits.
About 90% attack success with five malicious texts per target question in a knowledge base of millions. The authors found the defences they tested insufficient.

flashcards.front: Name two ingest-time controls for poisoning.
flashcards.back: Source authentication with write control, and provenance fields plus a trust tier on every chunk, so retrieval can exclude low-trust content for high-stakes queries.
